In [[queueing theory]], a discipline within the mathematical [[probability theory|theory of probability]], a '''BCMP network''' is a class of [[queueing theory|queueing network]] for which a [[product-form solution|product-form equilibrium distribution]] exists. It is named after the authors of the paper where the network was first described: [[Forest Baskett|Baskett]], [[K. Mani Chandy|Chandy]], Muntz, and Palacios. The theorem is a significant extension to a [[Jackson network]] allowing virtually arbitrary customer routing and service time distributions, subject to particular service disciplines.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Baskett | first1 = F. | last2 = Chandy | first2 = K. Mani | author2-link = K. Mani Chandy | last3 = Muntz | first3 = R.R. | last4 = Palacios | first4 = F.G. | title = Open, closed and mixed networks of queues with different classes of customers | journal = Journal of the ACM | volume = 22 | issue = 2 | pages = 248&ndash;260 | year = 1975 | doi = 10.1145/321879.321887 | s2cid = 15204199 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The paper is well known, and the theorem was described in 1990 as "one of the seminal achievements in queueing theory in the last 20 years" by [[J. Michael Harrison]] and [[Ruth J. Williams]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Harrison | first1 = J.M. | author-link = J. Michael Harrison | last2 = Williams | first2 = R.J. | title = On the Quasireversibility of a Multiclass Brownian Service Station | journal = The Annals of Probability | volume = 18 | issue = 3 | pages = 1249&ndash;1268 | publisher = Institute of Mathematical Statistics | year = 1990 | jstor = 2244425 | doi = 10.1214/aop/1176990745 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Definition==
A network of ''m'' interconnected queues is known as a '''BCMP network''' if each of the queues is of one of the following four types:

# [[First-come, first-served|FCFS]] discipline where all customers have the same [[Exponential distribution|negative exponential]] service time distribution. The service rate can be state dependent, so write <math>\scriptstyle{\mu_j}</math> for the service rate when the queue length is ''j''.
# Processor sharing queues
# Infinite-server queues
# [[LIFO (computing)|LCFS]] with pre-emptive resume (work is not lost)

In the final three cases, service time distributions must have [[rational function|rational]] [[Laplace transform]]s. This means the Laplace transform must be of the form<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cnx.org/content/m10853/latest/|title=BCMP Theorem|first=Bart|last=Sinclair|publisher=Connexions|access-date=2011-08-14}}</ref>
:<math>L(s) = \frac{N(s)}{D(s)}.</math>

Also, the following conditions must be met.

# external arrivals to node ''i'' (if any) form a [[Poisson process]],
# a customer completing service at queue ''i'' will either move to some new queue ''j'' with (fixed) probability <math>P_{ij}</math> or leave the system with probability <math>1-\sum_{j=1}^{m}P_{ij}</math>, which is non-zero for some subset of the queues.

==Theorem==
For a BCMP network of ''m'' queues which is open, closed or mixed in which each queue is of type 1, 2, 3 or 4, the equilibrium state probabilities are given by

:<math>\pi(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_m) = C \pi_1(x_1) \pi_2(x_2) \cdots \pi_m(x_m),</math>

where ''C'' is a normalizing constant chosen to make the equilibrium state probabilities sum to 1 and <math>\scriptstyle{\pi_i(\cdot)}</math> represents the equilibrium distribution for queue ''i''.

===Proof===
The original proof of the theorem was given by checking the [[independent balance equation]]s were satisfied.

[[Peter G. Harrison]] offered an alternative proof<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Harchol-Balter | first1 = M.|author1-link=Mor Harchol-Balter | chapter = Networks with Time-Sharing (PS) Servers (BCMP) | doi = 10.1017/CBO9781139226424.029 | title = Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems | pages = 380–394 | year = 2012 | isbn = 9781139226424 }}</ref> by considering reversed processes.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Harrison | first1 = P. G. | author-link = Peter G. Harrison | doi = 10.1016/j.laa.2004.02.020 | title = Reversed processes, product forms and a non-product form | journal = Linear Algebra and Its Applications | volume = 386 | pages = 359–381 | year = 2004 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
